(a) the mammary tumor contains only 10% as much desaturase activity as the corresponding tissue of the lactating mouse, and (b) the desaturase activity of the tumor is unaltered by the type of diet consumed by the host.

the oleate levels in mammary tumors of C3H/He mice were not altered by the type of diet consumed by the mice, whereas oleate levels in liver were greatly increased by a linoleate deficient diet, and the specific activity of steraoyl-CoA delta 9 desaturase in hepatic microsome was increased by a linolae deficient diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the metabolism of fatty acids by mammary tumors, and the effects of dietary factors on the fatty acid composition of the tissue and the stearoyl CoA desaturase.
a study of the metabolism of linoleic and oleic acids in mammary adenomatous tissues of C3H/HeJ mice and in their corresponding liver tissues.

a better understanding of the metabolic and biochemical basis for the differences in the growth of tumors in animals fed diets with various fatty acid compositions and the role of dietary fat in tumor growth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stearoyl desaturase activity of the mammary tumor microsome is not affected by dietary manipulation.
the desaturase activity is enhanced in the liver of mice fed a high carbohydrate, low fat diet, but is not altered in a mammary adenocarconoma.
mammary tumor cells are not capable of desaturating stearate to oleate, and that the oleate present in the tumor is derived from the diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the desaturation of stearic acid in mammary tumors is not dependent upon dietary manipulation, and that the increased desaturation of fatty acids in liver microsomal fractions from mice fed a fat free, high carbohydrate diet is due to the absence of dietary linoleate.
the stearoyl CoA desaturase is not a tumor specific enzyme, but is a dietary regulated enzyme.
the mammary adenocarconoma of C3H strain mice does not have the ability to synthesize oleate from stearate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the desaturase activity is not a general phenomenon in neoplastic tissue.
dietary adaptation of stearoy-CoA desaturases is not a general property of neoplastic tissues.

the desaturation of stearate to oleate is an essential process in the biosynthesis of fatty acids and that the lack of this process leads to an increase in saturated fatty acid levels in the body, which has been linked to several diseases.
